A laid hedge is not a planted one. You take what is already growing, cut most of the way through each stem near the base, bend it over at an angle, and weave it between stakes. The stem stays alive because the cut is partial. In a season the horizontal growth throws up vertical shoots along its whole length, and what was a line of separate trees becomes one continuous barrier that a bullock cannot push through.

The cut is the part people get wrong. Too shallow and the stem springs back or snaps when you bend it; too deep and the connection dies over winter and you have a dead stick in a line of living ones. The right depth leaves roughly a fifth of the stem intact, and there is no way to learn it except by ruining perhaps forty stems and then not ruining the forty-first.

Regional styles are mostly arguments about livestock. A Midland bullock hedge is built thick and brushy on the field side because a bullock leans. A Welsh double-brush hedge is built for sheep, which do not lean but do squeeze. The stake spacing, the angle of the pleach and which way the brush faces all follow from what animal is meant to be stopped by it.

Timing matters more than technique. Cut between November and March, when the sap is down and the birds have finished. A hedge laid in September will bleed, and one laid in May destroys nests you cannot see from the outside. This is not a preference; in most of the country it is the law, and the law is right.

The reason to do any of it is that a laid hedge lasts fifty years and a fence lasts fifteen, and the hedge is meanwhile a linear woodland running through a field. It costs more per metre up front, roughly four times more, and the arithmetic only works if you intend to still be farming the same field when the fence would have needed replacing for the third time.
